analysis.one_liner: Blocked EPA carbon rules on power plants until most other countries passed equally strict limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee or floor vote and died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017, so no EPA carbon rule was ever blocked by it.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have amended the Clean Air Act so that no EPA rule limiting carbon dioxide from fossil-fuel power plants could take effect until the EPA certified that countries responsible for at least 80% of the world's carbon emissions (not counting the United States) had adopted regulations at least as strict, with the same numeric limits and deadlines [S2] [S3]. Because few if any countries write identical numeric standards, that bar was effectively out of reach, so the bill would have indefinitely delayed US power-plant carbon limits [S2] [S3]. It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, where no further action was taken; it died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies and coal- and gas-fired electric utilities would have gained the most: an EPA carbon rule for power plants could not take effect, so plants would face no federal carbon limits and no compliance costs under such a rule [S2] [S3]. Coal-producing regions whose jobs and tax bases depend on those plants would have been shielded, at least for a time, from plant closures and electricity price increases that supporters of the bill associated with EPA regulation [S3] [S1].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal and fossil-fuel power plant operators

how_it_helps.text: It would have given coal- and gas-fired power plants an indefinite reprieve from EPA carbon limits: no rule concerning carbon dioxide from fossil fuel-fired generating units could take effect until the EPA certified that countries emitting at least 80% of the world's non-US carbon dioxide had adopted equally strict rules, on the same numeric standards and timetables [S2] [S3].

It also contained a provision declaring that nothing in the law should be read as giving the EPA any authority over carbon dioxide emissions, going beyond delay to try to close the door on carbon regulation generally [S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, ordinary people would have borne the costs: continued carbon emissions from power plants contributing to climate change, and continued conventional air pollution from coal-fired generation that carbon rules might have accelerated the cleanup or retirement of. Households in other regions would also have kept paying for climate-related damages while coal regions kept the jobs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households, through pollution and climate harm

drawbacks.text: The core drawback is the one the bill itself acknowledges by its structure: it would have made US climate action hostage to other countries' laws. Requiring 80% of non-US global emissions to be covered by rules with equal numeric standards and timetables is a bar no country's regulation is likely to meet, so the practical effect was to stop EPA carbon rules for power plants rather than coordinate them [S2] [S3].

The good-faith case for it, reflected in its title and the sponsors' framing, was fairness to coal communities: unilateral EPA rules could raise electricity prices and cost jobs in coal-dependent areas like Pennsylvania and West Virginia while other major emitters kept emitting freely [S1] [S3]. An honest supporter would concede that the bill offered no alternative plan for power-plant emissions or for the workers and regions it aimed to protect [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated benefit — protecting coal jobs and ratepayers from unilateral EPA regulation — was real for coal-dependent regions but narrow, and it came at the price of blocking any federal carbon limit on the nation's largest stationary source of carbon dioxide, with no substitute policy. The design, requiring foreign laws to match US numeric standards exactly, made the protection effectively permanent rather than a waiting period. Weighed honestly, the gains went to a specific industry while the costs — pollution and climate risk — were spread across everyone.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in a House subcommittee after referral, never got a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Keith Rothfus introduced the bill on December 3, 2015, with 11 Republican cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1] [S4] [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, where the action record ends — no hearing, markup, or vote is listed [S5].
The 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, and the bill expired without ever reaching the House floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died in committee, EPA carbon regulation of power plants was never blocked by this statute, so ordinary people exposed to power-plant pollution and anyone favoring federal carbon limits are better off than they would have been had it passed; the coal interests the bill was written to protect gained nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary people, since the bill died in committee

for.name: Rep. Keith Rothfus
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the House floor

for.name: 11 Republican cosponsors
for.role: Cosponsors, including Reps. McKinley (WV), Cramer (ND), and Zinke (MT)

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership (Chair Fred Upton)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or floor action after it was referred to the Energy and Power Subcommittee; the action record shows nothing after the subcommittee referral

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans and no Democrat supported it; the bill never advanced far enough for any recorded vote.

industries.note: The bill would have blocked EPA carbon rules that pressure coal-fired plants toward retirement, protecting coal demand and mining jobs. Its gain came at the cost of continued power-plant pollution and climate harm borne by the public [S2] [S3].

Fossil fuel-fired generating units were the bill's named subject; operators would have avoided compliance costs from any EPA carbon rule taking effect. Because the bill died, these costs were never lifted [S3].

Carbon rules on fossil plants are a main driver of the shift toward renewables and efficiency; indefinitely delaying them would have slowed that market shift. The bill died, so this effect never occurred [S2] [S3].
